pr_title: nspawn: ensure single-process container running as --user can access credentials
pr_body:
When starting a container with --user, the new uid will be resolved and switched to only in the inner child, at the end of the setup, by spawning getent. But the credentials are set up in the outer child, long before the user is resolvable, and the directories/files are made only readable by root and read-only, which means they cannot be changed later and made visible to the user.

When this particular combination is specified, it is obvious the caller wants the single-process container to be able to use credentials, so make them world readable only in that specific case.

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/31794
pr_comments:
While this works fine when also using `--no-new-privs` and `--drop-capabilities=all`, I think there are conceivable use cases where the spawned command is able to elevate its privileges via suid and spawn other processes that maybe should not be able to access the credentials. Is that a relevant corner case? If not, should the new behavior be documented along the `--user` option?

The particular use case I had in mind does use `--no-new-privs` and thus is safe regarding this method.
Added check for no-new-privs and documentation
hmm, i have no better idea, looks fine then.

issue_context.title: systemd-nspawn: combining --set-credential and --user does not work
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

255.4

### Used distribution

Debian bookworm+unstable

### Linux kernel version used

6.7.9-cloud-amd64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd-nspawn

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

I expected that setting a credential (via `--set-creential` or `--load-credential`) would be accessible to the initial process created by `systemd-nspawn` inside the container. This is the case when running as `root`, but when changing the user via `--user`, accessing credentials results in `Permission denied`.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

_No response_

### Steps to reproduce the problem

I don't think the container distribution or version matters much. I opted for using Debian bookworm here as all that is needed from inside is a working `systemd-creds`.

   # TARGET=/tmp/target
    # debootstrap --variant=minbase --include=systemd bookworm "$TARGET"
    ...
    # useradd --root "$TARGET" --create-home user
    # systemd-nspawn --directory "$TARGET" --read-only --set-credential=secret:hunter2 systemd-creds list
    Spawning container target on /srv/target.
    Press Ctrl-] three times within 1s to kill container.
    NAME   SECURE SIZE PATH                  
    secret secure   7B /run/host/credentials/secret
    Container target exited successfully.          
    # systemd-nspawn --directory "$TARGET" --read-only --set-credential=secret:hunter2 --user user systemd-creds list
    Spawning container target on /srv/target.
    Press Ctrl-] three times within 1s to kill container.
    Failed to open credentials directory '/run/host/credentials': Permission denied
    Container target failed with error code 1.
    #

I would have expected that the second `systemd-nspawn` invocation to also show me the credential.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_

review_comments: i'd really prefer we we'd chown the creds to the target user instead?
As the comment says, we get a username, but we can't resolve it until much later, so don't know how to do that. it's single process invocations with NNP, so there shouldn't be issues in principle?
